title: Homeschooling: Not Just For Hippies and Religious People Anymore
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss homeschooling in the United States: its history alongside compulsory school attendance laws, why families choose it, state-by-state legal and tax differences, practical questions to weigh before starting (cost, qualifications, child's input), notification and record requirements (using North Carolina as an example), teaching methods (classical/trivium, Montessori, Charlotte Mason narration, Waldorf, unit studies, unschooling, eclectic), learning styles, college admission concerns, and socialization. They are joined by Kristen Conger of Stuff Mom Never Told You, who was homeschooled from second through eighth grade and describes her family's experience. The episode closes with listener mail about Wiltshire, England, and a local legend about moon rakers.

segments.title: Opening banter and history of compulsory schooling
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about their educator parents and whether they were raised with opinions on homeschooling. They recount the history of compulsory school attendance, from Massachusetts in 1852 to Mississippi as the last state in 1918, and the grassroots start of the modern homeschool movement.

segments.title: Why families homeschool and state laws
segments.summary: Discussion of reasons parents homeschool, including concerns about school environment, religious or moral reasons, and dissatisfaction with instruction. The hosts note that homeschool laws differ by state and there is no federal law.

segments.title: Taxes, vouchers and public school funding
segments.summary: The hosts discuss tax credits for homeschool expenses in some states, such as Louisiana, Illinois, and Minnesota, California treating homeschools as private schools, and tuition vouchers that can fund homeschooling. They also describe the funding tension between public schools and homeschooling families, and the growth in the number of homeschooled students.

segments.title: Questions to ask before homeschooling: why, cost, and who teaches
segments.summary: Chuck cites recommended books and says the first questions are why and whether the family can afford it. They discuss opportunity cost of a parent's lost salary, alternatives such as grandparents teaching, and whether a parent is qualified to teach.

segments.title: Talking with the child and checking state rules
segments.summary: The hosts advise an honest dialogue with the child about homeschooling and note it can be tried for a trial period. They then cover checking state requirements, using North Carolina as an example with its notice of intent, teacher diploma requirement, attendance, immunizations, and testing rules, and note that some states have minimal requirements and others are highly regulated such as New York.

segments.title: Homeschool teaching methods
segments.summary: Overview of teaching approaches: structured state curriculum or school-at-home, classical education and the trivium stages, Montessori, Charlotte Mason narration, Waldorf (head, heart, hands), unit studies, unschooling, and the eclectic method, with the observation that many families become less rigid over time.

segments.title: Learning styles and choosing a method
segments.summary: The hosts describe four learning modalities (visual, auditory, tactile, kinesthetic) and advise identifying the child's learning style and the parent's teaching style, then observing what works.

segments.title: College admission, socialization and research
segments.summary: The hosts say homeschool advocates claim homeschooled students have an easier time getting into college, though they found no quantitative evidence for this. They discuss keeping records, homeschool co-ops and groups for clubs and sports, and the socialization concern, citing research and a thesis by Thomas Smedley. They list famous people said to have been homeschooled.

segments.title: Guest interview: Kristen Conger's homeschool experience
segments.summary: Kristen Conger, a colleague from Stuff Mom Never Told You, describes being homeschooled from second through eighth grade by her mother, a former public high school teacher, in a religious family. She covers the curriculum her mother used, social activities such as soccer, ballet and church youth group, her return to regular high school, and her siblings' college experience. She says she would not homeschool her own children.

segments.title: Listener mail: Wiltshire moon rakers legend
segments.summary: A listener from Salisbury, Wiltshire, near Stonehenge, writes about the Wyndham Arms pub and its Crop Circle ale, and shares the local legend of the moon rakers, whose bootleggers hid their booze in a pond and claimed they were raking out a cheese, which is the origin of the nickname. The hosts thank the listener and say they will send a shipping address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and the website reference.
